title: Iran Strategic Intelligence Report 2026: A Regime Under Siege
excerpt: A deep 2026 intelligence assessment of Iran after the assassination of Ali Khamenei - the contested rise of Mojtaba Khamenei, the IRGC's tightening grip, nuclear hedging without enforcement, and a regime fighting for survival on every front.
content:
Iran Strategic Intelligence Report 2026: A Regime Under Siege

No state in the world has had a stranger, more violent 2026 than Iran. It has lost its Supreme Leader to assassination for the first time in the Islamic Republic's history. It has watched a hereditary succession unfold inside a system explicitly built to reject hereditary rule. It has absorbed the deepest military strikes on its territory since the Iran-Iraq War, lost dozens of senior commanders and nuclear scientists in a single opening salvo, and still found the capacity to keep fighting - through missiles, drones, a counter-blockade of its own coastline, and a network of regional proxies stretched thinner than at any point in a generation. Iran in 2026 is not a defeated state. It is a wounded, internally fractured, externally weakened state that has nonetheless refused to break, and understanding exactly how it has survived, and at what cost, is essential to reading the next phase of Middle Eastern geopolitics.

This report examines Iran's strategic position with full attention to the most consequential development in the Islamic Republic's recent history: the killing of Ali Khamenei and the contested rise of his son, Mojtaba, to the position of Supreme Leader - a succession that tells us more about where real power now sits in Tehran than any official statement coming out of the country.

Executive Summary

On February 28, 2026, joint American-Israeli strikes under Operation Epic Fury killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, ending his thirty-seven-year tenure and triggering Iran's first ever leadership crisis at the apex of the Islamic Republic's clerical system. Within ten days, in an opaque and pressured process, the Assembly of Experts confirmed Mojtaba Khamenei - Ali Khamenei's second son, a midlevel cleric with no published religious scholarship, no government office, and no recognized qualification as a marja-e taqlid - as the Islamic Republic's third Supreme Leader. The succession, reportedly driven by intense pressure from Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders on Assembly of Experts members in the chaotic days after the assassination, represents what regional analysts increasingly describe as a quiet but decisive transfer of real power away from the clerical establishment and toward the IRGC itself, with Mojtaba serving less as an independent religious authority and more as a legitimizing figurehead for a security apparatus that now runs the country.

Iran's military and economic position has deteriorated sharply through the year's fighting. The 2026 Iran war, beginning with Operation Epic Fury and continuing in various forms through the June 17 Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, killed dozens of senior IRGC and Quds Force commanders alongside Khamenei, including figures Trump himself acknowledged were on Washington's own list of likely successors - "second or third place is dead," as he put it. Iran's proxy network - Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis, and Iraqi militias collectively known as the Axis of Resistance - has been degraded across the board, with Hezbollah absorbing over a thousand confirmed IRGC-linked operative losses in Lebanon and Hamas losing successive military chiefs to Israeli strikes inside Gaza. Iran's economy remains under crushing sanctions pressure, its oil exports disrupted by both Israeli strikes on energy infrastructure and its own counter-blockade standoff with the United States in the Strait of Hormuz. And the country's domestic political situation remains explosive: the late 2025 to early 2026 uprising, met with brutal repression, has not been extinguished, even as the regime doubles down on coercion rather than reform under its new, contested leadership.

Yet for all of this, Iran has not collapsed, and even Israeli officials have privately acknowledged there is no certainty the war will bring down the regime. The IRGC has demonstrated a command structure resilient enough to absorb catastrophic leadership losses and maintain operational continuity - what Gulf-based analysts describe as a system explicitly adapted to survive a decapitation scenario. Iran's strategic posture for the remainder of 2026 and beyond will be defined by this central tension: a regime stripped of religious legitimacy and led by a figure many Iranians view as the installation of hereditary monarchy inside a republic founded explicitly to reject monarchy, but one that retains coercive capacity, nuclear hedging infrastructure, and a security establishment determined to survive through hardening rather than accommodation.

Background

Iran's 2026 crisis did not emerge from nowhere. It is the culmination of a confrontation that has been building since the collapse of the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action and accelerated dramatically with the June 2025 Twelve-Day War, in which Israel's Operation Rising Lion struck Iran's Natanz enrichment facility, killed senior nuclear scientists and military leadership, and was followed by American strikes on three Iranian nuclear sites before a ceasefire took hold on June 24, 2025. That war did not resolve the underlying dispute over Iran's nuclear program; it deepened Iranian distrust of any negotiated settlement and accelerated internal debate over succession, as Khamenei - already elderly and reportedly in declining health for years - began quietly preparing contingency plans for his own death while sheltering during the conflict.

Domestically, Iran entered 2026 already in crisis. A mass uprising that began in late December 2025 and continued through February 2026 was met with a brutal government crackdown, including the arrest of key reformist politicians - a pattern consistent with previous uprisings in 2017, 2019, and 2022, but occurring this time against a backdrop of acute economic strain from sanctions and the lingering damage of the 2025 war. It was into this combustible domestic environment that the February 28 strikes landed.

Khamenei had, according to multiple reports including those from The New York Times, made informal preparations for his own succession in the weeks before his death, reportedly naming Chief Justice Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, his longtime chief of staff Asghar Hijazi, and Hassan Khomeini - grandson of revolutionary founder Ruhollah Khomeini - as his preferred candidates in case of assassination. None of this had been formalized or publicly disclosed. When the strikes came on February 28, Israeli intelligence proved devastatingly precise: Hijazi was reportedly killed, along with Ali Larijani and dozens of other senior officials Trump later said had been on his own administration's list of likely successors. "The attack was so successful it knocked out most of the candidates," Trump told ABC News. "It's not going to be anybody that we were thinking of because they are all dead. Second or third place is dead."

Current Situation

The Succession: Mojtaba Khamenei and the IRGC's Quiet Coup

Under Article 111 of Iran's constitution, the sudden vacancy at the top triggered the formation of an Interim Leadership Council on March 1, comprising President Masoud Pezeshkian, Chief Justice Mohseni-Eje'i, and Guardian Council jurist Alireza Arafi. The Assembly of Experts, the eighty-eight-member clerical body constitutionally tasked with selecting a new Supreme Leader, convened in emergency session from March 3 to 8 - reportedly under direct, sustained pressure from IRGC commanders, who according to Iran International made "repeated contacts and psychological and political pressure" on Assembly members in the days before the vote, attempting at points to bypass the formal electoral process altogether. On March 9, the Assembly announced Mojtaba Khamenei as Iran's third Supreme Leader.

The selection is, by any honest reading, constitutionally and theologically irregular. Iran's constitution requires a Supreme Leader to possess deep scholarly religious credentials as a source of Islamic jurisprudence; Mojtaba, a midlevel cleric who left the seminary years ago, has published no scholarly religious work and has never been recognized by any senior cleric - any marja-al taqlid - as possessing the independent juristic authority the office formally requires. He has never held elected or government office. His primary qualifications are bloodline and decades of quiet, informal influence over Iran's security and intelligence apparatus through what insiders call the "Leadership House," a parallel structure of offices linked directly to the Supreme Leader's office that has functioned, by multiple accounts, as an unofficial coordination point between the IRGC and the political leadership for years.

Most strikingly, Ali Khamenei himself had reportedly opposed his son's candidacy for years. In 2017, he explicitly condemned hereditary rule as a form of monarchical restoration - comparing the transfer of power from father to son to passing down "a copper ablution pot used in the bathroom from one shah to another" - and repeatedly barred his sons from entering the economic sphere, warning he would sever ties if they exploited their proximity to power. That historical record makes Mojtaba's installation, in the chaotic aftermath of his father's assassination, all the more revealing: it was not a reformist consensus choice, nor the fulfillment of any clearly designated succession plan, but the product of IRGC commanders and hardline figures including Saeed Jalili moving decisively to install a figure they viewed as reliable, pliable, and capable of preserving internal cohesion during wartime - while reformists led by figures like former Presidents Mohammad Khatami and Hassan Rouhani, lacking comparable access to Assembly of Experts members, had no real mechanism to contest the outcome.

Gulf-based analysts have characterized this plainly: the succession does not represent uncontested religious authority or a new political phase, but rather "continuity under pressure" - a formalization of the regime's ongoing re-entrenchment around its security apparatus. Mojtaba inherits the machinery of repression and Iran's nuclear and missile programs, but not his father's religious stature or capacity to manage the regime's internal contradictions. The most important conclusion for any strategic analyst tracking Iran going forward: the real locus of power in post-Khamenei Iran is the IRGC, not the new Supreme Leader. Mojtaba functions as the legitimizing face of an institution that has effectively absorbed final authority over wartime decision-making, internal security, and repression.

The Military Picture: Degraded but Not Destroyed

Iran's military and proxy network absorbed extraordinary punishment through the 2026 war. Operation Epic Fury's opening salvo alone involved close to 900 strikes in twelve hours, killing not just Khamenei but dozens of senior IRGC and Quds Force commanders - a level of leadership decapitation without precedent in the regime's history. Iranian human rights monitors estimated at least 657 people killed and over 2,000 wounded from related strikes, with credible reporting suggesting the true toll across the full conflict, including Lebanon-related fighting, runs considerably higher.

Yet Iran's retaliatory capacity proved more durable than many expected. Tehran sustained missile and drone strikes against Israel, American forces, and Gulf states for months, recording over 660 distinct attack events against Gulf targets alone by early April, with the UAE absorbing the heaviest impact and Kuwait recording the highest casualties. Iran weaponized the Strait of Hormuz directly, alternately threatening closure, harassing shipping, and ultimately finding itself in a "dual blockade" standoff once the United States imposed its own naval blockade in April - a confrontation that disrupted global oil markets for weeks and forced a coordinated G7 Strategic Petroleum Reserve release.

Iran's broader Axis of Resistance has fared worse. Hezbollah, despite mounting a genuinely sustained resistance in southern Lebanon - over 260 attacks in May alone - has lost more than a thousand fighters by the IDF's own count and remains besieged across multiple fronts in southern Lebanon, with no clear path to rebuilding its pre-war capability while under continuous Israeli ground pressure. Hamas has lost successive military chiefs, including Izz al-Din Haddad and his immediate replacement Mohammed Odeh, in a campaign of targeted killings that has continued even during the nominal Gaza ceasefire. The Houthis, while retaining the capacity for symbolic strikes, have shown caution about full-scale escalation into the Red Sea given the risk of inviting direct Israeli retaliation. Taken together, Iran's regional proxy architecture - built over decades as the central pillar of its deterrence and power-projection strategy - has been substantially, though not completely, dismantled in operational terms.

The Nuclear File: Hedging Without Verification

Iran's nuclear program sits at the center of the unresolved strategic picture. The IAEA has stated it found no evidence of an active weaponization program, but has also been unable to verify Iran's actual enrichment status or stockpile levels since the original 2025 strikes, because Iran has refused to permit inspections of damaged sites. In February 2026, Iran formally informed the IAEA that normal safeguards had become "legally untenable and materially impracticable" given the scale of attacks against its nuclear infrastructure and personnel - a position the Iranian parliament reinforced by voting to suspend the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran's cooperation with the agency entirely in mid-2025.

British and American analysts, along with the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, characterize Iran's current posture as deliberate nuclear hedging: maintaining the technical infrastructure and enriched uranium stockpile necessary to assemble a weapon on short notice, without crossing into actual weaponization, using the ambiguity itself as negotiating leverage. Iranian officials have signalled willingness to dilute or export higher-enriched uranium in exchange for sanctions relief and credible guarantees against future attacks - exactly the kind of transactional bargain the Islamabad MOU gestures toward without actually locking in. The MOU's fourteen-point framework commits Iran not to acquire a nuclear weapon, echoing language from the defunct JCPOA, but contains no enforcement mechanism, leaving IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi's warning that an agreement without real inspection provisions amounts to an "illusion of an agreement" as the central unresolved question hanging over the entire settlement.

Economy and Sanctions: A Country Running on Fumes and Leverage

Iran's economy remains under severe strain. Years of sanctions, compounded by the direct costs of the 2025 and 2026 wars - destroyed energy infrastructure, disrupted oil exports, and a counter-blockade standoff that froze significant volumes of seaborne trade for weeks - have left the country dependent on a narrowing set of economic relationships, chiefly with China, which continues to absorb the bulk of Iran's sanctioned oil exports through opaque shadow-fleet arrangements. The dual blockade earlier in 2026 forced reduced traffic through Hormuz to a trickle - at one point only fifteen ships made it through the strait in a roughly two-week window - with direct knock-on effects for Iran's own export revenue at precisely the moment the regime most needed hard currency to fund both the war effort and domestic security operations against renewed unrest.

The June 2026 discussion within the Trump administration over redirecting Iran's frozen overseas assets toward Gulf state reconstruction costs, and Trump's own dismissive June 16 comment that controlling Iran's nuclear material isn't particularly "valuable" since alternatives exist, both signal a Washington negotiating posture explicitly designed to keep maximum financial pressure on Tehran even as the shooting war winds down. For a regime now led by a figure whose own family wealth - Bloomberg has reported on Mojtaba Khamenei's access to Swiss bank accounts and British luxury property worth over $100 million despite standing US sanctions since 2019 - stands in stark and politically dangerous contrast to the economic desperation driving repeated waves of domestic unrest, this financial squeeze carries genuine destabilization potential that goes well beyond conventional sanctions pressure.

Strategic Analysis

Iran's 2026 strategic position can be summarized as catastrophic in leadership terms, resilient in coercive-capacity terms, and unresolved in nearly every dimension that matters for the medium term. The killing of Ali Khamenei and the rushed, IRGC-engineered installation of Mojtaba represents the single most significant rupture in the Islamic Republic's governing structure since the 1979 revolution itself - more consequential, in institutional terms, than even the death of founder Ruhollah Khomeini in 1989, because that earlier transition at least followed an orderly, pre-arranged constitutional process. What Iran has now is something closer to a managed institutional crisis dressed in the language of continuity: a Supreme Leader without genuine religious authority, propped up by a security apparatus that has effectively become the regime's actual center of gravity.

This matters enormously for how outside powers should read Iranian behavior going forward. A Mojtaba-led, IRGC-dominated Iran is likely to be more, not less, hardline in its external posture, precisely because the new leadership lacks the religious legitimacy to make the kind of consequential, system-altering compromises - a genuine nuclear deal, a fundamental opening to the West - that even Ali Khamenei occasionally proved capable of when cornered. Gulf analysts' warning that Mojtaba "offers no departure from the past" in foreign policy, and that a regime unable to resolve its internal legitimacy crisis will "turn outward through aggression and inward through repression," reflects a structurally sound read of incentives: a leadership installed by security hardliners has every reason to keep the security hardliners satisfied, and very little independent political capital to spend on conciliation.

At the same time, Iran's demonstrated resilience under extraordinary military pressure should not be read as strength so much as institutional adaptation to weakness. The IRGC's command structure, explicitly built and tested to absorb decapitation strikes and maintain continuity, kept the war machine functioning even as senior leadership was eliminated wholesale. But resilience purchased through coercion and repression rather than legitimacy carries a compounding cost. Each crackdown against domestic unrest, each demonstration that succession runs through IRGC pressure rather than genuine clerical consensus, narrows the regime's base of organic support and increases its long-term dependence on raw coercive capacity - a survival strategy with a shelf life, even if that shelf life cannot be precisely dated.

The proxy network's degradation compounds this problem geopolitically. Iran built its regional deterrence architecture specifically to avoid having to fight conventional wars on its own soil by projecting power through Hezbollah, Hamas, Iraqi militias, and the Houthis. With Hezbollah devastated, Hamas's leadership repeatedly decapitated, and Assad's fall in Syria having already removed a key logistical corridor, Iran now faces a starker, more direct exposure to Israeli and American military pressure than at any point since the Islamic Republic's founding - precisely the strategic encirclement its entire post-1979 foreign policy was designed to prevent.

Global Impact

Iran's weakened position has reshaped the wider Middle East's balance of power in ways that extend well beyond its own borders. Russia's conspicuous failure to materially defend either Khamenei's leadership or Iran's broader war effort - despite decades of strategic partnership and Iranian drone supplies that proved central to Russia's own war against Ukraine - has visibly damaged Tehran's confidence in its great-power patron, even as both states continue performing partnership rhetorically. This mirrors a broader pattern across Russia's client network in 2026, from the collapse of the Assad regime in Syria to Moscow's near-total silence following the American capture of Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro, suggesting Iran can no longer assume meaningful Russian backing in a genuine crisis.

China's role has, by contrast, become more economically central even as it remains militarily and diplomatically cautious. Beijing continues absorbing the overwhelming majority of Iran's sanctioned oil exports and was reportedly involved in elements of the truce negotiations process, reflecting China's broader interest in regional stability that protects its own energy supply lines and Belt and Road-linked infrastructure investments, without any indication Beijing is prepared to extend the kind of security guarantees that might deter further Israeli or American action.

For Gulf Arab states, Iran's weakened posture has accelerated a broader recalibration already visible in the UAE's decision to exit OPEC and align more closely with American energy policy during the war. A Gulf increasingly confident that Iran's capacity for coercive regional disruption has been structurally degraded is likely to continue diversifying its security relationships and reducing the leverage Tehran has historically extracted through the implicit threat of Hormuz disruption or proxy attack - even as the events of 2026 demonstrate that threat has not been entirely eliminated.

For India and the wider Indo-Pacific, Iran's instability carries direct and tangible consequences. India's Chabahar port investment, long positioned as a strategic alternative trade and connectivity corridor bypassing Pakistan, sits directly exposed to continued Iranian political instability and the unresolved sanctions environment. Continued volatility in the Strait of Hormuz sustains elevated energy security risk for India's substantial Gulf-sourced oil imports, reinforcing the broader case for accelerated energy diversification that New Delhi has been pursuing across Russian, American, and African sources in recent years.

Risk Assessment

  • Legitimacy crisis triggering renewed mass unrest: Mojtaba Khamenei's installation, widely perceived domestically as the imposition of hereditary monarchy inside a republic founded to reject it, carries genuine potential to reignite the uprising that was suppressed in early 2026, particularly if economic conditions continue deteriorating under sustained sanctions pressure.
  • Covert nuclear reconstitution: With IAEA inspections suspended and no verified enforcement mechanism in the Islamabad MOU, the risk that Iran's surviving enrichment infrastructure is used to covertly reconstitute weapons-relevant capability under a leadership with less to lose diplomatically remains substantial and largely unmonitored.
  • IRGC factional fragmentation: A succession installed through internal IRGC pressure rather than genuine institutional consensus carries inherent fragility; competing power centers within the Guards, the Basij, and remaining clerical establishment figures could produce destabilizing internal power struggles, particularly if Mojtaba proves unable to manage the same balancing act his father sustained for decades.
  • Proxy network desperation escalation: A severely weakened Hezbollah and Hamas, facing existential pressure, carry elevated risk of high-casualty, high-visibility attacks designed to demonstrate continued relevance and deter further Israeli operations - a dynamic that historically increases rather than decreases short-term violence even as overall capability declines.
  • Strait of Hormuz recurrence: The underlying dispute that produced the dual-blockade standoff - Iranian insistence on linking Hormuz access to broader regional ceasefire terms, particularly regarding Lebanon - remains unresolved beneath the Islamabad MOU's sixty-day window, leaving renewed disruption to global energy markets a live possibility once that window closes.
  • Loss of strategic depth: With Syria lost, Hezbollah devastated, and Hamas isolated, Iran's traditional doctrine of forward deterrence through regional proxies has been structurally undermined, potentially pushing a cornered leadership toward more direct, higher-risk forms of confrontation in the absence of its preferred asymmetric tools.
The most dangerous version of post-Khamenei Iran is not necessarily a stronger one - it is a weaker, more cornered one led by figures with less religious legitimacy to lose and a security establishment with every institutional incentive to prove its continued relevance through confrontation rather than concession.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis

The following are illustrative projections based on current trajectories and institutional dynamics, intended for strategic stress-testing rather than presented as confirmed predictions.

Scenario One: Hardened Survival Under IRGC Control (45% probability)

Mojtaba Khamenei consolidates a largely ceremonial leadership role while the IRGC formalizes its position as the regime's actual governing authority, managing both the nuclear hedging strategy and continued, lower-intensity proxy operations through Hezbollah's remnants and residual Houthi capability. Domestic unrest is contained through sustained repression rather than resolved, sanctions pressure continues, and Iran settles into a more militarized, less internationally engaged version of the Islamic Republic - weakened regionally but not collapsed.

Scenario Two: Internal Fragmentation and Power Struggle (25% probability)

Mojtaba's lack of independent religious authority and political base proves unsustainable, triggering competing IRGC factional alignments or a more assertive push from reformist-aligned clerical figures like Hassan Khomeini to challenge the succession's legitimacy. This produces a period of internal Iranian political instability that, while falling short of regime collapse, significantly degrades Tehran's capacity for coherent external strategy and creates opportunities for renewed mass protest to gain traction.

Scenario Three: Renewed Conflict Over Nuclear Reconstitution (20% probability)

Intelligence indicating covert Iranian efforts to reconstitute enrichment capability beyond the Islamabad MOU's terms, in the absence of restored IAEA verification, triggers a second round of Israeli strikes - potentially with reduced or no direct American military participation given Washington's stated preference for diplomatic closure on the file. This tests whether Iran's post-war command structure, still rebuilding from Operation Epic Fury's losses, can mount an effective response, and whether the new leadership's legitimacy can survive a second major military humiliation.

Scenario Four: Negotiated Opening Under Pressure (10% probability)

Combined economic desperation, sustained domestic unrest, and the practical limits of IRGC-only governance push the regime toward a more substantive nuclear and regional settlement than the current MOU provides - potentially involving real IAEA verification in exchange for meaningful sanctions relief - as the least-bad option for regime survival, with Hassan Khomeini or reform-aligned figures gaining limited but genuine policy influence as part of the bargain.

Intelligence Forecast

Global Chanakya's assessment for the coming twelve to eighteen months centers on several interlocking dynamics. First, watch the IRGC-Mojtaba relationship closely: any visible friction between the nominal Supreme Leader and the security establishment that installed him would be the clearest early signal of the succession's underlying fragility. Second, expect continued, low-visibility domestic repression rather than either full regime collapse or genuine political opening, as the path of least institutional resistance for a leadership with limited legitimacy and maximum coercive capacity. Third, expect the nuclear file to remain the central flashpoint, with the absence of restored IAEA verification creating a recurring crisis trigger every time fresh intelligence, credible or contested, suggests Iranian enrichment activity beyond agreed limits. Fourth, expect Iran's proxy network to prioritize survival and reconstruction over major new offensive operations in the near term, given the scale of losses absorbed across Hezbollah, Hamas, and the broader Axis of Resistance through 2026 - though sporadic, demonstrative attacks designed to signal continued relevance should be expected rather than ruled out. Fifth, expect China's economic role to deepen further as Iran's primary lifeline, even as Beijing continues avoiding any security commitment that would draw it into direct confrontation with the United States or Israel over Iran's future.

For India specifically, the practical forecast implications are clear: continued caution around Chabahar-linked investment timelines given Iran's unresolved internal instability, sustained attention to Hormuz-related energy security risk through at least the remainder of 2026, and close monitoring of how a more IRGC-dominated Iranian foreign policy approach affects India's careful, historically balanced relationships with both Tehran and the Gulf Arab states simultaneously.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Iran in 2026 has suffered the most consequential leadership rupture in the Islamic Republic's history and emerged from it not reformed, not collapsed, but reconfigured around its security apparatus in ways that will likely make it more rigid, more coercive, and less capable of the kind of substantive diplomatic compromise that could genuinely resolve its standoff with Israel and the United States. Mojtaba Khamenei's installation as Supreme Leader is, stripped of its religious framing, an IRGC consolidation of power dressed in clerical robes - a regime choosing institutional survival through coercion over the harder, riskier path of genuine legitimacy renewal. The strategic question that will define the region for years to come is whether a security establishment with everything to lose and a shrinking proxy network to project power through chooses managed retrenchment, or doubles down on confrontation precisely because confrontation, however costly, remains the only language in which it has ever known how to assert relevance. Every other actor in the region - Israel, the Gulf states, the United States, and watchful powers further afield including India - will spend the next several years calibrating their own posture around the answer to that single question.

title: Narendra Modi's Strategic Global Influence: India's 2026 Playbook
excerpt: A deep 2026 assessment of Narendra Modi's global strategic footprint - from surviving Trump's tariff war and Operation Sindoor's aftermath to record diplomatic outreach and India's high-wire multialignment act among the US, Russia and China.
content:
Narendra Modi's Strategic Global Influence: India's 2026 Playbook

There is a particular kind of diplomatic skill required to be simultaneously sanctioned by punitive American tariffs, photographed warmly with Vladimir Putin, courted by Xi Jinping's China, and still treated by Washington as an indispensable Indo-Pacific partner - all within the same eighteen-month window. Narendra Modi has spent 2025 and 2026 doing exactly that, and the fact that India has emerged from a year of genuine diplomatic turbulence with its strategic autonomy intact, its economy still growing faster than any major power, and its global standing arguably enhanced rather than diminished, says as much about the architecture Modi has built over twelve years as it does about any single decision made this year.

This report examines Modi's strategic global influence in 2026 with the analytical rigour the subject demands - not the celebratory framing of government communiqués, nor the dismissive framing of critics, but a clear-eyed assessment of what India's multialignment strategy has actually delivered, where it has been tested to its limits, and where the cracks are beginning to show.

Executive Summary

Narendra Modi enters the second half of 2026 as India's longest continuously serving elected Prime Minister, having completed his hundredth foreign trip in June and crossed 4,399 consecutive days in office. The numbers tell only part of the story. The substantive test of 2026 has been whether Modi's signature foreign policy doctrine - strategic autonomy expressed through simultaneous engagement with Washington, Moscow, Beijing, the Gulf, and the Global South - could survive its most serious stress test yet: a brutal 2025-26 trade and diplomatic crisis with the Trump administration that saw tariffs on Indian goods climb to a punishing 50%, among the highest imposed on any American trading partner, driven explicitly by India's continued purchase of discounted Russian crude.

That crisis has, by mid-2026, been substantially though not fully resolved. A February 2026 trade agreement brought tariffs down to 18%, and the punitive 25% Russia-linked surcharge was formally lifted on February 7 following India's gradual diversification away from Russian crude - imports fell to a thirty-eight-month low by December 2025 even as American oil purchases rose 31% year-on-year. But the relationship's underlying volatility, and the political cost Modi absorbed domestically - opposition leader Rahul Gandhi's "Narendra Surrender" jibe captured a genuine public unease about agricultural sector concessions - illustrate the real limits of even India's most carefully constructed great-power balancing act. Modi's parallel management of relationships with Putin's Russia, Xi Jinping's China, and a expanding web of partnerships across the Gulf, Europe, ASEAN, and the Pacific Islands demonstrates a foreign policy apparatus more institutionally mature and less personality-dependent than it was a decade ago, even as it remains, by design, heavily centered on Modi's own direct diplomatic engagement.

The deeper strategic story of 2026 is India's successful, if costly, navigation of what regional analysts call a genuine "multialignment test" - managing simultaneous, often contradictory pressures from a US-China trade truce, a fragile Russia-Ukraine peace process, an unresolved West Asian crisis disrupting energy markets, and India's own unresolved security relationship with Pakistan in the aftermath of Operation Sindoor. India has not been forced to choose a single bloc or patron, which remains the central achievement of Modi-era foreign policy. But 2026 has made unmistakably clear that strategic autonomy in an era of transactional great-power politics carries real, rising costs - costs India is increasingly being asked to absorb in tariffs, trade concessions, and diplomatic capital rather than simply rhetorical friction.

Background

To understand Modi's 2026 positioning, it is necessary to trace the doctrine he has built since 2014. India's foreign policy under Modi shifted decisively from what foreign policy analysts describe as a traditionally reactive, "rule-blocker" posture rooted in Cold War-era non-alignment toward a proactive, "problem-solving rule-shaper" approach - engaging simultaneously with the United States, Russia, China, the Quad, BRICS, the Gulf states, and the Global South without binding India permanently to any single axis. This is what Indian strategists now formally call multialignment, distinct from the older non-alignment doctrine in that it actively seeks deep, simultaneous partnerships across blocs rather than equidistant abstention from all of them.

The doctrine's institutional anchors have been consistent: the "Neighbourhood First" policy aimed at stabilizing South Asia; the "Act East" policy deepening ties with Southeast Asia and the Indo-Pacific as a structural counterweight to China; an increasingly assertive security posture toward cross-border terrorism, visible in the post-Uri surgical strikes, the Balakot air strikes, and most recently Operation Sindoor; and a deliberate, sustained investment in personal diplomacy, with Modi having received 32 of the world's highest national honours and addressed sixteen foreign parliaments over his tenure. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, appointed in 2019, has been a critical institutional stabilizer, allowing India to weather an increasingly turbulent global environment with consistent, professionally articulated positions even as Modi's own personal diplomacy with leaders ranging from Trump to Putin to Xi has occasionally proven more volatile than the institutional relationships beneath it.

2025 set the stage for 2026's tests directly. Following the Pahalgam terror attack and the subsequent four-day India-Pakistan conflict in May 2025, India launched Operation Sindoor against terrorist targets in Pakistan, reaching a ceasefire after intense but contained military exchanges. President Trump's repeated public claims that he personally mediated the ceasefire - claims India has consistently and firmly rejected - became a genuine point of friction. According to reporting from the investment bank Jefferies, the unusually punitive tariff regime that followed was, in significant part, driven by Trump's personal frustration at India's refusal to credit him with brokering peace, a refusal widely read in Washington as costing him a plausible Nobel Peace Prize narrative. Former National Security Advisor John Bolton's blunt assessment - calling the tariffs and Trump's mediation claims "inappropriate" - reflected a broader unease among American foreign policy veterans that decades of bipartisan effort to build the US-India relationship were being damaged by what amounted to personal pique.

Current Situation

The US Relationship: From Crisis to Costly Stabilization

The defining bilateral story of Modi's 2026 has been the management of the US-India trade and diplomatic crisis that began in August 2025. President Trump's executive order that August imposed a 25% tariff explicitly tied to India's continued imports of Russian crude oil, stacking on top of an existing 25% reciprocal tariff to produce a punishing 50% total - placing India, as commentator Fareed Zakaria pointed out at the time, in the same tariff category as Syria and Myanmar, while Pakistan, despite its close ties to China, received considerably more favourable treatment. Trump's public description of India's economy as "dead" and Indian tariffs as "obnoxious" represented an unusually personal and public rupture in what had been one of the more carefully tended great-power relationships of the post-Cold War era.

India's response combined quiet economic adjustment with public assertion of strategic autonomy. The Ministry of External Affairs's consistent position - that "ensuring the energy security of 1.4 billion Indians is the supreme priority" and that diversifying energy sourcing according to "objective market conditions" is a sovereign decision - never wavered publicly even as, behind the scenes, India's Russian crude imports fell to a thirty-eight-month low by December 2025. This combination of public firmness and private flexibility is a recurring signature of Modi-era crisis management: never appearing to capitulate to external pressure while quietly adjusting policy to manage genuine economic costs.

The February 2026 trade agreement reduced the reciprocal tariff from 25% to 18% and formally lifted the Russia-linked 25% surcharge effective February 7, bringing India's effective tariff rate down from a peak of 50% to 18% - still higher than India's regional competitors Vietnam and Bangladesh face, but a substantial de-escalation. The deal sparked genuine domestic controversy, particularly around agricultural sector concessions, with opposition leader Rahul Gandhi's "Narendra Surrender" framing capturing a real vein of public discontent about whether India had conceded too much, too publicly, after months of asserting it would not bow to pressure. Trump's claim that India had agreed to halt Russian crude purchases entirely and pivot toward American and potentially Venezuelan oil was notably never officially confirmed by New Delhi - another characteristic pattern, where Washington's public framing of concessions tends to run ahead of India's actual, more carefully hedged commitments.

Russia: The Relationship Washington Cannot Break

Despite the entire tariff crisis being explicitly framed around Russian oil purchases, the Modi-Putin relationship has remained visibly intact through 2026. Putin's December 2025 visit to India came at the height of US tariff pressure, a deliberate signal that India would not allow Washington to dictate the terms of its Moscow relationship even under significant economic duress. This is not sentimentality; it reflects hard strategic calculation. Russia remains India's primary source of military hardware across multiple legacy platforms, a relationship decades in the making that cannot be quickly substituted, and discounted Russian crude - even at reduced volumes - has provided India with genuine fiscal savings during a period of elevated global energy price volatility driven by the parallel Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruptions covered elsewhere in Global Chanakya's Middle East coverage.

The "Modi-Putin selfie" that US Representative Sydney Kamlager-Dove cited as evidence of Trump's tariff strategy backfiring captures something real: the harder Washington pushed India on Russia, the more visible and demonstrative India's continued engagement with Moscow became - a pattern consistent with India's longstanding refusal to let external powers dictate the architecture of its strategic partnerships.

China: Pragmatic De-escalation Without Resolution

India's relationship with China remains the most structurally unresolved of Modi's major-power balancing acts. Personal informal engagement between Modi and Xi Jinping has continued, though as analysts at the Vivekananda International Foundation note, this informal diplomacy has yielded limited concrete dividends on the core disputes - the unresolved Line of Actual Control border tensions, China's deepening relationship with Pakistan, and broader Indo-Pacific strategic competition. What 2026 has demonstrated is a more interesting, second-order dynamic: American tariff pressure on India has had the paradoxical effect of pushing India and China marginally closer on select economic fronts, even as the underlying strategic rivalry between New Delhi and Beijing remains fully intact. India's March 2026 Cabinet approval of amendments easing Press Note 3 restrictions on foreign direct investment from border-sharing nations - widely understood to mean China - signals a pragmatic, if cautious, economic recalibration happening in parallel with continued strategic wariness.

The Diplomatic Calendar: Unprecedented Density

The sheer density of Modi's 2026 diplomatic engagement reflects both the doctrine's maturity and the genuinely unusual convergence of global crises this year. His June two-nation tour of France and Slovakia - the latter a first-ever visit by an Indian Prime Minister since Slovak independence in 1993 - marked his hundredth foreign trip since 2014, a milestone underscoring just how central direct, leader-level diplomacy remains to India's foreign policy execution. Earlier in the year, a five-nation tour covering the UAE, Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, and Italy unfolded almost in parallel with the Trump-Xi Beijing summit, a BRICS foreign ministers' gathering hosted in New Delhi, and Quad foreign ministers convening in the Indian capital - a genuine convergence of major-power diplomatic activity onto Indian soil that analysts have described as the most consequential simultaneous test yet of India's capacity to engage multiple poles at once without losing strategic coherence.

This diplomatic density has not been without domestic political tension. Modi's call for Indians to limit non-essential foreign travel in 2026 to conserve foreign exchange reserves amid global economic uncertainty drew pointed criticism from opposition figures given his own status as India's most travelled Prime Minister - a minor but telling illustration of the gap between India's expansive global diplomatic posture and the more constrained economic realities facing ordinary Indian citizens as the full impact of the US tariff regime continued working through the economy.

Israel and the Gulf: A Quietly Deepening Partnership

Modi's February 2026 visit to Israel - his second as Prime Minister following the historic first visit in 2017 - underscored a personal closeness with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that has persisted even as Israel's conduct of simultaneous wars against Iran, Hezbollah, and within Gaza has drawn intensifying international criticism, including from several of India's own European partners. This relationship, alongside continued deep engagement with the UAE and Saudi Arabia, reflects India's pragmatic, interest-based approach to the Middle East: deepening defence, technology, and energy cooperation with Israel and the Gulf monarchies simultaneously, while maintaining careful rhetorical balance on the Palestinian question consistent with India's traditional position, and largely avoiding the kind of public alignment controversies that have entangled European partners more directly in the Gaza and Lebanon conflicts.

Strategic Analysis

The defining strategic insight from Modi's 2026 performance is that multialignment, as a doctrine, has proven durable under genuine pressure - but not free. The US tariff crisis represents the most serious test of India's strategic autonomy doctrine in the Modi era, considerably more consequential than periodic friction with China or earlier trade disputes, precisely because it came from India's most important strategic partner and was explicitly designed to force a binary choice between American market access and Russian energy and defense ties. India's refusal to make that binary choice, even while absorbing a punishing 50% tariff for roughly six months, represents a genuine demonstration of strategic resolve that will likely be studied by other middle powers navigating similar great-power pressure in the years ahead.

But resolve alone did not resolve the crisis - economic adjustment did. India's gradual, unannounced reduction in Russian crude purchases, reaching a thirty-eight-month low by December 2025, demonstrates that Modi's strategic autonomy doctrine operates through quiet, incremental recalibration rather than dramatic public reversal. This is, in many ways, the doctrine's core operating logic: never publicly concede to pressure, but adjust enough substantively to make de-escalation possible on terms India can credibly describe as sovereign choice rather than capitulation. Whether this pattern will remain sustainable against a Trump administration that has shown a clear willingness to use tariff leverage as a primary instrument of geopolitical coercion - visible equally in its China trade war and its broader "model ally" burden-sharing framework detailed in Global Chanakya's coverage of US strategic doctrine - is one of the genuinely open questions for the remainder of Modi's term.

The China dimension reveals a parallel strategic logic operating on a longer time horizon. India's pragmatic economic recalibration toward China, even amid continued strategic distrust, reflects an emerging recognition within Indian policy circles that excessive dependence on any single great-power relationship - even the US relationship that has anchored Indo-Pacific strategy for two decades - carries genuine vulnerability, as 2025-26's tariff crisis demonstrated in stark terms. A India that diversifies its economic relationships even with strategic rivals, while maintaining firm security and defence postures against those same rivals, is executing a more sophisticated, risk-distributed version of multialignment than the simpler "balance the US against Russia and China" framework that dominated earlier analysis of Indian foreign policy.

Domestically, the blurring of foreign policy, domestic politics, and economic management that regional analysts predicted for 2026 has materialized precisely as forecast. The political cost of the February trade deal, crystallized in Rahul Gandhi's "surrender" framing, illustrates that Modi's foreign policy successes can no longer be cleanly insulated from domestic political scrutiny the way they often were in his first two terms. As the tariff regime's full economic impact continues working through Indian agricultural and manufacturing sectors, the government's capacity to offset foreign policy friction with purely domestic political wins - state election victories, GST reforms, labour code changes - will be tested more directly than at any point in the past decade.

Global Impact

India's 2026 strategic positioning carries consequences well beyond its own borders. For the Quad - the US, Japan, Australia, and India - New Delhi's demonstrated willingness to absorb significant economic pressure from Washington rather than abandon its Russia relationship sends an important signal about the practical limits of American expectations for Indo-Pacific partners. This matters directly for how Tokyo and Canberra calibrate their own relationships with Washington, particularly as the broader American doctrine of conditional, transactional alliance management - detailed extensively in Global Chanakya's assessment of 2026 US grand strategy - increasingly treats burden-sharing and political alignment as preconditions for full security cooperation.

For BRICS and the broader Global South, India's continued ability to maintain deep ties with both Russia and China while simultaneously deepening relationships with the US, EU, Israel, and the Gulf reinforces New Delhi's self-positioned role as the credible voice for 125 developing nations through its Voice of Global South Summits framework - a positioning Modi has consciously and consistently cultivated since India's G20 presidency, using initiatives like the International Solar Alliance and the international expansion of India's Unified Payments Interface digital infrastructure to demonstrate tangible South-South cooperation rather than purely rhetorical solidarity.

For Pakistan, the continued, if currently dormant, tension following Operation Sindoor remains a persistent undercurrent shaping India's broader regional posture. The relative restraint both sides exercised after November 2025 terror attacks in New Delhi and Islamabad - neither triggering renewed military action - reflects what regional analysts describe as mutual strategic caution fuelled by external pressure and nuclear deterrence, though the risk of unplanned escalation remains genuinely elevated given persistent hyper-nationalist rhetoric on both sides and the unpredictability of non-state armed actors operating across the border.

For Europe, India's expanding diplomatic engagement - the EU-India FTA covering tariff concessions on 99% of India's trade value, the unprecedented density of 2026 European visits, and deepening technology and defence cooperation - reflects a genuine European interest in diversifying partnerships away from excessive China dependence, with India positioned as the most credible large-economy alternative, even as European unease about aspects of India's domestic political trajectory under BJP governance occasionally complicates the relationship's full potential.

Risk Assessment

  • Renewed US tariff escalation: Trump's repeated threats to raise tariffs on India to as high as 500% should Russian crude purchases resume at scale represent a standing risk that could resurface the entire 2025-26 crisis dynamic, particularly given the administration's demonstrated willingness to use trade policy as a primary geopolitical lever across multiple relationships simultaneously.
  • Domestic political costs compounding: As tariff-related economic pain continues working through agricultural and manufacturing sectors, the political sustainability of Modi's "absorb pressure quietly, adjust incrementally" strategy faces genuine testing, particularly with opposition framing around the February trade deal already demonstrating real public traction.
  • Pakistan escalation risk: Despite current restraint, the combination of hyper-nationalist domestic rhetoric in both India and Pakistan, unresolved Kashmir-linked grievances, and the demonstrated unpredictability of non-state militant actors creates persistent risk of an accidental or deliberate escalation that could force a more disruptive Indian military response than Operation Sindoor.
  • China relationship structural fragility: Economic pragmatism on FDI and trade coexists uneasily with unresolved border tensions and China's deepening strategic partnership with Pakistan; any Line of Actual Control flare-up would immediately strain the careful economic recalibration underway.
  • Energy security exposure: Continued Middle East volatility, detailed extensively in Global Chanakya's Iran and Israel coverage, sustains direct exposure for India given its 87% crude oil import dependence and the practical limits of how quickly Russian crude can be replaced without cost or supply disruption.
  • Multialignment fatigue: The sheer density of simultaneous, often competing diplomatic demands - managing the US, Russia, China, Gulf, European, and Global South relationships concurrently, each with distinct and sometimes contradictory expectations - creates genuine bandwidth and coherence risk for India's foreign policy apparatus, however institutionally mature it has become.
India's 2026 record demonstrates that strategic autonomy is not free - it is a doctrine that must be actively defended, at real economic cost, against great powers increasingly willing to weaponize trade and market access as instruments of geopolitical coercion.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis

The following scenarios are illustrative projections based on current trajectories, offered for strategic stress-testing rather than as confirmed predictions.

Scenario One: Stabilized Multialignment (50% probability)

The February 2026 US trade agreement holds, India continues gradual energy diversification without fully abandoning Russian crude, and the China relationship proceeds along its current dual-track path of economic pragmatism alongside continued strategic wariness. Modi's foreign policy apparatus successfully manages the dense 2026 diplomatic calendar without major rupture, and India enters 2027 with its multialignment doctrine intact, if more expensively defended than in previous years.

Scenario Two: Renewed US-India Friction (25% probability)

Trump administration pressure resumes over continued Russian energy ties, a fresh trade dispute emerges over agricultural market access or technology transfer terms, or a personality-driven friction point similar to the 2025 mediation-claim dispute resurfaces, triggering renewed tariff escalation. India responds with further diversification toward Gulf and African energy sources while deepening BRICS and Global South coordination as a hedge, accelerating a gradual, structural cooling of US-India economic interdependence even as security cooperation continues.

Scenario Three: South Asian Security Shock (15% probability)

A significant cross-border terror attack, exceeding the scale of the November 2025 incidents, forces a more disruptive Indian military response than Operation Sindoor, drawing in renewed international mediation pressure and testing India's careful balancing act between firm security responses and continued global diplomatic engagement, particularly given Pakistan's deepening relationship with both China and elements of the Trump administration's business and diplomatic networks.

Scenario Four: Accelerated Strategic Diversification (10% probability)

Sustained unpredictability from Washington pushes India toward a more decisive structural pivot - deeper BRICS financial architecture engagement, accelerated indigenous defence production to reduce both American and Russian platform dependence, and a more assertive Global South leadership role - representing a genuine, rather than incremental, recalibration of India's traditional reliance on US-anchored Indo-Pacific security architecture.

Intelligence Forecast

Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on several converging dynamics. First, expect continued US-India trade relationship volatility even after the February 2026 agreement's stabilizing effect - the underlying tension between Washington's expectation of full Russian energy disengagement and India's insistence on sovereign energy diversification remains structurally unresolved and likely to resurface periodically. Second, expect India's economic engagement with China to continue deepening pragmatically on trade and investment fronts even as strategic and security competition remains fully intact - a genuine bifurcation between economic and security tracks that will require careful ongoing analysis rather than a single unified "China policy" framework. Third, expect Modi's diplomatic travel intensity to continue at a record pace through the remainder of 2026, with particular attention warranted to any additional Indo-Pacific outreach given the convergence of Quad coordination, ASEAN engagement, and the broader American Indo-Pacific alliance architecture detailed in Global Chanakya's US strategic coverage. Fourth, watch the domestic political dimension closely: as the 2025-26 tariff crisis's full economic costs continue working through Indian markets, opposition criticism of Modi's foreign policy management is likely to intensify rather than fade, particularly ahead of state elections where agricultural and trade policy concerns carry direct electoral weight. Fifth, expect continued Indian restraint on the Pakistan front barring a major escalatory trigger, with Operation Sindoor's precedent now established as the calibrated, proportionate response template for future cross-border provocations short of an attack large enough to demand a more decisive military response.

For Indian strategic planners specifically, the central lesson of 2026 is that multialignment's durability depends increasingly on India's capacity for quiet, continuous economic adjustment rather than purely diplomatic skill - the doctrine survives not because India successfully avoids pressure from any single great power, but because it has built enough genuine optionality across multiple relationships to absorb pressure from any one of them without being forced into full dependency on, or full rupture with, any other.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Narendra Modi's 2026 record demonstrates both the genuine strength and the rising cost of India's multialignment doctrine under conditions of intensifying great-power transactionalism. India absorbed the most punishing American tariff regime imposed on any major economy this year, maintained its Russia relationship through the pressure rather than abandoning it, continued a careful economic recalibration with China without compromising security vigilance, and sustained an unprecedented density of global diplomatic engagement - all while managing real domestic political costs and a still-unresolved security relationship with Pakistan. This is not the record of a foreign policy doctrine in crisis; it is the record of a doctrine being genuinely tested, under real pressure, and largely holding. The strategic question for the remainder of Modi's term, and for whoever eventually succeeds him, is whether India's multialignment model remains sustainable as more great powers, not just Washington, begin treating trade access and strategic partnership as conditional, transactional instruments rather than stable, rules-based commitments - a shift in the global operating environment that Global Chanakya's parallel coverage of US, China, and Russian strategic doctrine in 2026 suggests is no longer the exception, but rapidly becoming the new global norm.
