title: Donald Trump's Foreign Policy Predictions: The Doctrine of Disruption
excerpt: A definitive 2026 intelligence assessment of Donald Trump's foreign policy doctrine - from the Iran war and Venezuela operation to the China trade truce, the systematic downgrade of European alliances, and what comes next across every major theatre the Trump administration has upended.
content:
Donald Trump's Foreign Policy Predictions: The Doctrine of Disruption

There is a particular kind of analytical paralysis that sets in when you are trying to study a leader who treats unpredictability as a strategic asset. Every framework you apply, he walks out of. Every red line you draw, he tests. Every prediction you make, he violates - and then, sometimes, accidentally validates by doing exactly what the framework predicted for entirely different reasons than the model assumed. Donald Trump's foreign policy in his second term has produced this paralysis in institutionalists, realists, and liberal internationalists alike, and that paralysis is, in Global Chanakya's assessment, itself a significant strategic outcome - one that Trump has leveraged, consciously or intuitively, to extract concessions that more predictable administrations could never have generated.

But unpredictability is not the same thing as incoherence, and the eighteen months since Trump's return to the White House have produced enough evidence to identify the doctrine beneath the disruption. The sprawl of activity, unmatched by any modern American President, is the Trump Doctrine in action: American power as a lever deployed at will, subject to change at his whim, concentrated not in institutions but in the person of the President himself. This report decodes that doctrine systematically - not to endorse or condemn it, but to give the strategic planners, diplomats, investors, and analysts in India, the Indo-Pacific, Europe, the Gulf, and every capital that must navigate a Trump-shaped world the clearest possible picture of what this administration has done, why it has done it, and what it is likely to do next.

Executive Summary

Donald Trump's second-term foreign policy has, in eighteen months, executed five broad strategic planks simultaneously: shoring up the Western Hemisphere, maintaining a favorable balance of power in Asia, delegating European defense to the Europeans, delegating Middle East stability to regional coalitions, and using U.S. energy and deregulation to supercharge U.S. competitive technologies. These planks are not accidental; they emerge from the 2025 National Security Strategy and the 2026 National Defense Strategy in coherent, if bluntly stated, form. What makes them disorienting for traditional allies and rivals alike is their execution style: coercive, transactional, deeply personality-driven, and willing to deploy force, tariffs, and diplomatic rupture as first-order instruments rather than last resorts.

The administration's ledger after eighteen months is genuinely mixed in ways that neither its defenders nor its critics are entirely comfortable acknowledging. On the win side by its own accounting: a covert operation captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, removing one of Russia's last Western Hemisphere footholds; joint strikes with Israel in Operation Epic Fury killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and significantly degraded Iran's nuclear command structure; a US-China tariff war was de-escalated into a one-year truce after the Beijing summit; European NATO members have been forced, for the first time in decades, to take defence spending seriously; the Gaza ceasefire, however incomplete, ended the most intensive phase of combat in that conflict. On the loss side: the Iran war produced more casualties, more Gulf disruption and more diplomatic cost than the administration's optimistic pre-war framing anticipated; the US-China truce contains no resolution of the core technology rivalry; Ukraine peace remains elusive; there have been more than 350,000 deaths attributed to foreign aid cuts since January as America's global development footprint collapsed; and Russia and China have emerged from 2025 more confident that they can achieve their geopolitical goals.

The central intelligence forecast Global Chanakya draws from this record: as the Trump administration approaches the midterm elections, the need to energize core supporters could make it even less institutionally anchored, more transactional, and more focused on short-term political wins - making 2026's second half potentially more volatile and more personally driven than the first half, as domestic political calculations increasingly filter every foreign policy decision through the lens of a president who has never clearly distinguished between America's strategic interests and his own political survival needs.

Background

Trump's foreign policy worldview has three intellectual roots, and understanding each separately helps explain what would otherwise appear as random, disconnected disruption. The first root is transactionalism as philosophy - a deeply held conviction, predating his political career and visible in his 1987 book The Art of the Deal, that every relationship in life is fundamentally a negotiation, that every partner is either overpaying or underpaying, and that the primary purpose of American power is to correct those imbalances in America's favour. From this perspective, NATO allies who spend less than 2% of GDP on defence are not partners who deserve solidarity - they are freeloaders who deserve pressure. Trade partners with surpluses against the United States are not integrated economies benefiting from open markets - they are exploiters deserving tariffs. Even adversaries are potential deal partners if they can be brought to the table on sufficiently favourable terms.

The second root is hemispheric primacy as instinct. Trump's invocation of the Panama Canal, the acquisition of Greenland, the capture of Maduro, and the strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean reflect not a coherent Monroe Doctrine revival but something older and more visceral: a belief that the United States' immediate neighbourhood is its unchallengeable domain, that Chinese influence in the Panama Canal is an affront, and that Russian presence in Venezuela is an imposition to be removed rather than a political reality to be managed. The National Security Strategy can be viewed as a framework for proactively managing that gap, both by increasing the means at the United States' disposal through rewired trade relationships, rebalanced alliances, and mobilization of hemispheric resources, and by reducing the immediate ends or threats to which those means would need to be applied through strategic diplomacy, détente, and deterrence.

The third root is personal power concentration as operating principle. While Trump's unpredictability can be a liability, it is also his leverage. World leaders fear his wrath and adjust their behavior to avoid provoking him. This is not accidental; it is Trump's most consistent foreign policy tool. By making himself the sole credible channel for American commitment and the sole threat of American punishment, he has created a negotiating environment in which every foreign government must manage not a bureaucratic process with predictable institutional constraints, but a single individual whose preferences, moods, and personal relationships determine outcomes in ways that no amount of analytical modelling can fully anticipate.

Current Situation

The Western Hemisphere: Consolidation Through Force

The most dramatic single action of Trump's foreign policy in 2026 was also its most legally and normatively controversial: the January 2 capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in Caracas, executed through covert American military and intelligence action, with Maduro and his wife transported to New York to face narco-trafficking charges in the Southern District. On January 2, 2026, the U.S. carried out an attack on Venezuela's capital of Caracas. According to White House social media posts, the U.S. military captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife and took them out of the country.

The operation's strategic logic was explicit from the administration's own communications: Venezuela had become a node in a Russia-Iran-China network of sanctioned-regime cooperation in the Western Hemisphere, and its removal served the Donroe Doctrine's central objective of expelling rival great-power influence from the Americas. Russia's near-total public silence after Maduro's capture - despite Moscow's decades-long relationship with Caracas and Putin's personal ties to Maduro - confirmed what the administration had calculated: that Moscow, overextended by Ukraine and unable to project meaningful force across the Atlantic, had effectively abandoned its Latin American client network. Trump also committed billions to bail out an Argentine President, freed a former Honduran President convicted of drug trafficking, and approved strikes that killed more than 95 people on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific, raising accusations of war crimes. This is hemispheric primacy in practice: no legal instrument too blunt to deploy, no partner too unsavoury to embrace, no normative constraint worth preserving if it conflicts with the objective of making the Western Hemisphere unambiguously American strategic territory.

The Middle East: Force Forward, Diplomacy Improvised

Operation Epic Fury, launched February 28 in coordination with Israel, was the Trump administration's most consequential single military action and its clearest demonstration of both the doctrine's strengths and its structural limitations. The strikes killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and devastated Iran's senior military and nuclear command structure - a historical achievement by any military standard. In rapid succession, Trump bombed militants in Yemen and Iranian nuclear facilities, midwifed a fragile ceasefire in Gaza, forced European leaders to increase their defence spending, and extracted commercial and strategic pledges from China.

But the war's aftermath confirmed the gap between tactical success and strategic resolution that runs through every Trump foreign policy action. The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed June 17 lacks verified enforcement mechanisms. Trump admitted publicly to manipulating market expectations by repeatedly claiming a deal was imminent before one existed. He acknowledged accepting terms "far short of unconditional capitulation" he had originally demanded, citing fear of economic catastrophe from sustained Hormuz disruption. And his decision to spend critical ceasefire-negotiation hours at a UFC event rather than at the bargaining table - leaving senior envoys including Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and JD Vance in Islamabad without his direct authority - illustrated how the personalisation of foreign policy creates its own operational vulnerabilities when the person himself is not present.

Trump's threat to "blow up" Oman on May 27, 2026 - stating publicly that "Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up" - captures the doctrine's most combustible dimension: the use of maximalist, unfiltered public threats as negotiating pressure, which simultaneously achieves short-term compliance and generates long-term credibility costs as partners and rivals calibrate how seriously to take any given statement.

China: The Truce That Resolved Nothing

The US-China relationship in 2026 has been the most consequential and least durably resolved of all the administration's major foreign policy files. The tariff war escalated to mutual duties exceeding 140% by April before the February Supreme Court decision striking down Trump's IAEA tariff authority forced a partial retreat to a flat 10% baseline. The May 12-15 Beijing summit - the first American presidential state visit to China since 2017 - produced a truce reducing American tariffs to 30% and Chinese tariffs to 10%, with China suspending its antitrust investigations into American technology firms as a goodwill gesture.

During his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump advocated for a stringent stance against China, proposing tariffs as high as 60% on Chinese goods. Upon assuming office, he implemented a more modest 10% tariff on Chinese imports, while imposing tariffs on goods from traditional allies such as Canada and Mexico. The pattern - more aggressive in campaign rhetoric, more transactional in actual execution - is the consistent signature of how Trump handles China: treating the relationship as a negotiation where mutual economic pain produces table access, not as a strategic rivalry where the ultimate objective is structural decoupling or Chinese containment.

He might be willing to make trade or regulatory concessions that benefit China - easing various tariffs, adjusting technology licensing rules, or allowing specific Chinese firms into U.S. markets - while framing the moves as victories. Even if Trump's concessions do not immediately compromise core U.S. national security interests, they could create accumulated vulnerabilities that China may exploit over time. This is the most precise articulation of the strategic risk in Trump's China management: that a president who measures success in deal-terms rather than long-term power-terms may gradually concede structural advantages while claiming transactional wins, leaving the United States worse positioned in the underlying technology and military competition that will determine 21st-century primacy.

Trump will spend 2026 staring down an ominous deadline. U.S. intelligence analysts are convinced China's leader Xi Jinping has ordered the People's Liberation Army to build the military forces it needs to invade Taiwan by 2027. Yet Taiwan barely featured in the Beijing summit agenda, and the administration has been simultaneously strengthening the US-Philippines defence relationship - explicitly reaffirming that the 1951 Mutual Defence Treaty extends to armed attacks on Philippine forces anywhere in the Pacific - while maintaining studied ambiguity on Taiwan's own defence guarantee, a gap that Xi Jinping's patient strategic planners will have noted carefully.

Europe and NATO: The Alliance Under Managed Pressure

No relationship has been more systematically tested by the Trump doctrine than the transatlantic alliance. Vice President JD Vance's February 2025 Munich Security Conference address - asserting that Europe's primary threats are internal, citing "erosions in free speech and democratic values" - set the tone for an administration that during the campaign said European allies "treat us actually worse than our so-called enemies," vowing not to defend NATO allies who did not meet the 2% GDP defence spending target.

Trump has strengthened and weakened US alliances simultaneously. He has prompted allies to spend more on defence and accept more of their own security burdens, but he has also left them hedging against US unpredictability. This is, in truth, the most consequential structural outcome of Trump's European policy: not alliance collapse, but a fundamental shift in how European capitals relate to Washington - no longer assuming American reliability as a given, but actively building independent capability and alternative frameworks precisely because they can no longer afford to. The UK-France "coalition of the willing" military hub commitment inside Ukraine, the EU's accelerating defence-industrial integration, France's persistent advocacy for European strategic autonomy - all of these are direct policy responses to the Trump administration's managed reduction of European security commitments, and all of them will outlast the Trump presidency regardless of its electoral outcome.

CFR Senior Fellows argue that the knock-on effects of Trump's trade policies have tested Washington's relationship with its closest allies, including Australia, Canada, Europe, Japan, and New Zealand. The application of tariffs to traditional allies - treating Canada and Mexico, then Australia, Japan, and the EU as trade adversaries requiring reciprocal pressure - has produced a structural reclassification of American partnerships in every capital's strategic planning: the United States under Trump is not an unconditional ally but a conditional one, whose support must be bought and maintained through continuous economic and political concessions.

Ukraine: The Peacemaker Who Cannot Make Peace

Trump campaigned on ending the Ukraine war within hours of taking office. It did not happen in hours, or weeks, or months, and as of mid-2026, the conflict remains unresolved in any meaningful sense. The year concluded with peace deals still out of reach in Ukraine and Sudan, and a three-phase ceasefire plan in Gaza effectively stalled. The Trump administration's Ukraine strategy has been characterised by intense personal engagement - frequent calls with Putin, the August 2025 Anchorage summit - combined with growing public frustration with Moscow's unwillingness to offer meaningful territorial compromise and an increasingly visible American sympathy for the European "coalition of the willing" framework as a de facto substitute for American leadership on Ukraine's security guarantees.

The structural problem is that Trump's peace strategy depends on personal relationships with both Putin and Zelensky that are, simultaneously, his greatest asset and his greatest liability. His belief that direct leader-to-leader engagement can cut through institutional complexity has produced genuine diplomatic access; his inability to separate personal relationship management from substantive policy has produced a process in which his public statements about imminent breakthroughs, repeatedly unfulfilled, have progressively eroded the credibility of any American commitment on Ukraine's future.

Foreign Aid: The Silent Strategic Catastrophe

No dimension of Trump's foreign policy receives less analytical attention relative to its actual strategic consequence than the systematic dismantling of America's global development and humanitarian footprint. Historically, the United States has represented over half of global official development assistance, providing over $63.3 billion in 2024. For fiscal year 2025, enacted foreign aid dropped to $38.4 billion. Funding for 2026 stands at $28.5 billion, with estimates as low as $8.1 billion including rescissions and cancellations. There have been more than 350,000 deaths attributed to aid cuts since January.

This is not a peripheral consideration - it is the single dimension of Trump's foreign policy most directly relevant to China's long-term competitive position. Every country in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, and the Pacific Islands that loses American development financing and health programming either fills that gap through its own resources or accepts the alternative: Chinese infrastructure investment, Chinese development loans, Chinese digital and technology systems. The Donroe Doctrine's hemispheric consolidation makes geopolitical sense on paper; its simultaneous abandonment of the soft-power infrastructure through which American influence was maintained across the Global South hands Beijing precisely the competitive advantage that the administration's security policy is simultaneously trying to prevent.

Strategic Analysis

The most honest assessment of Trump's foreign policy after eighteen months is that it has succeeded in disrupting established equilibria across virtually every major relationship and theatre, and that disruption has produced both genuine leverage gains and genuine strategic costs - often simultaneously, in the same action. The Venezuela operation removed a Russia-linked regime from the hemisphere and restored a credibility of American coercive power that had been questioned for a decade; it also set a precedent for extrajudicial regime change that every authoritarian rival is now citing as legitimation for their own similar instincts. The Iran strikes killed Khamenei and degraded his nuclear command; they also demonstrated that even a battered, isolated Iran can inflict enough pain through a single geographic chokepoint to force an American president to accept terms "far short of unconditional capitulation." The China tariff war generated real concessions; it also demonstrated to Beijing that a one-year truce, carefully managed, can buy China the technological self-sufficiency time its 15th Five-Year Plan requires.

The most consistent through line is Trump's belief that the United States has underused its power globally. The areas where Trump has succeeded on his own terms are pretty numerous. The question is: Are those successes actually good for the U.S. position over the long term? This is the question that any serious strategic assessment must sit with, and it does not have a clean answer in mid-2026. What can be said with confidence is that the Trump doctrine's success condition - generating transactional wins that can be politically framed as demonstrations of American strength - is fundamentally different from the success condition of the strategic competition it is simultaneously trying to manage, which is preserving a structural advantage over China, Russia, and Iran across a decade-plus horizon that extends well beyond any single administration's term.

Trump's tariff approach raises a worst-case concern: "stagflation" - a combination of higher inflation and recession. With U.S. consumers expected to wind up shouldering most of Trump's tariffs, sending the inflation contribution of tariffs up, the domestic economic feedback loop from foreign policy decisions is intensifying rather than resolving, and the administration is heading into midterm territory with precisely the kind of affordability anxiety that historically punishes the party in power.

Global Impact

Trump's foreign policy reverberations extend into every corner of the international system in ways that will outlast his presidency regardless of its electoral outcome. In Europe, the combination of tariff pressure, reduced security guarantees, and contemptuous public rhetoric from JD Vance has produced the most consequential acceleration of genuine European strategic autonomy since Charles de Gaulle. This is almost certainly a permanent structural shift - once European capitals have invested the political capital in building independent defence-industrial capacity and alternative security frameworks, they will not dismanttle those investments when Washington eventually returns to more conventional alliance management.

For the Indo-Pacific, the administration's strategic focus remains more coherent than in any other theatre. The Trump administration has moved to bolster the United States' alliance with the Philippines, framing it as vital to a "free, open, prosperous, and secure Indo-Pacific" amid rising Chinese assertiveness in the South China Sea, reaffirming that the 1951 Mutual Defence Treaty extends to armed attacks on Philippine forces anywhere in the Pacific. The sustained investment in Quad coordination, the Philippines defence relationship, and semiconductor supply chain diversification through initiatives like Pax Silica represent the more institutionally durable half of Trump's foreign policy - areas where bipartisan consensus, clear Chinese threat framing, and allied interest alignment produce a more stable, less personality-dependent policy architecture.

For India specifically, New Delhi sees more political space opening in Washington as Trump's domestic standing shows signs of erosion. India's strategy now turns on mobilizing traditional pro-India constituencies - the security establishment, the U.S. Congress, business groups, and diaspora networks - accelerating its diversification strategy, and fast-tracking trade talks with Europe while expanding economic links beyond the US. This is a sophisticated, adaptive response to Trump's volatility: not confrontation, not surrender, but a deliberate structural diversification that reduces long-term dependence on American good offices precisely because 2025-26 demonstrated so clearly that those good offices can be weaponised through tariffs with minimal warning and maximal economic impact.

For the Global South broadly, America's foreign aid collapse has created a soft-power vacuum that China is already filling methodically with infrastructure investment, digital systems, and development financing through BRI channels - a dynamic that, left unaddressed by subsequent administrations, will likely prove more consequential to the balance of global influence than any single military operation or trade deal the Trump era produced.

Risk Assessment

  • Taiwan crisis before midterms: Trump will spend 2026 staring down an ominous deadline, with U.S. intelligence analysts convinced China's leader Xi Jinping has ordered the PLA to build the military forces it needs to invade Taiwan by 2027. An administration whose primary Taiwan focus is on the trade truce rather than clear deterrence signalling risks Xi reading American ambiguity as opportunity, particularly as the Beijing summit deliberately left Taiwan off the agenda entirely.
  • Iran MOU collapse: The Islamabad MOU's fourteen-point framework lacks verified enforcement, contains no inspection mechanism, and was negotiated by an administration that publicly acknowledged manipulating market expectations throughout the process - a foundation of trust-deficit that makes any breakdown of the sixty-day provisions extremely likely without sustained diplomatic investment Trump has not demonstrated capacity to sustain.
  • Stagflation from tariff feedback: U.S. consumers bearing an estimated 67% of the tariff burden heading into midterm territory, with slowing growth and rising prices, could produce domestic political pressure that forces abrupt, politically motivated foreign policy reversals - particularly on China trade - that undermine the strategic logic the administration has invested eighteen months building.
  • Alliance credibility spiral: Each instance of publicly treating traditional allies as trade adversaries - tariffs on Australia, Japan, Canada, the EU - compounds into a structural credibility problem: partners who have reduced their strategic dependence on Washington are less available as coalition members in any future crisis requiring allied military cooperation, precisely when that cooperation may be most needed in a Taiwan or Baltic scenario.
  • Dollar dominance erosion: Watch for signs of eroding U.S. dollar dominance. No one quite knows when global investors and sovereigns will tire of financing U.S. debt, which now stands at more than $38 trillion, or nearly 125 percent of U.S. gross domestic product. A foreign policy built on tariff revenue as fiscal instrument depends on dollar primacy that the tariff policy itself, combined with unpredictable ally treatment, is gradually undermining.
  • Post-Trump doctrine vacuum: Watch to see whether any Republican leaders translate Trump's instincts into a more lasting doctrine - on alliances, on relations with autocratic adversaries, and on trade. A doctrine so concentrated in a single person's preferences and relationships carries a structural vulnerability: when that person is no longer in office, every relationship and every commitment reverts to negotiation from scratch, leaving partners with no reliable institutional continuity to anchor long-term strategic planning.
The Trump doctrine has produced genuine short-term leverage and genuine long-term strategic exposure in almost every theatre simultaneously - the most consistent pattern in a foreign policy explicitly designed to be inconsistent is that transactional wins and structural costs tend to arrive in the same package.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis

The following scenarios are illustrative projections based on current trajectories, structured for strategic stress-testing rather than presented as confirmed predictions.

Scenario One: Midterm-Driven Transactional Escalation (45% probability)

Heading into November 2026 midterms, the administration intensifies foreign policy action on highest-visibility issues - renewed Iran pressure if the MOU wobbles, additional Western Hemisphere operations to maintain the "strength" narrative, and continued China technology confrontation even within the trade truce's nominal framework. Domestic economic pain from tariff inflation generates political pressure, but the administration responds with foreign policy assertiveness rather than tariff retreat, betting that strength-projection frames better electorally than economic adjustment. European allies deepen their autonomy projects, India accelerates diversification, and Xi Jinping maintains patient patience through the midterm cycle.

Scenario Two: China Trade Truce Collapse (25% probability)

The one-year US-China truce breaks down before its natural expiry - triggered by a Taiwan arms sale announcement, an Entity List expansion covering a major Chinese firm, or a deterioration in the Trump-Xi personal relationship - restarting tariff escalation above 100% and significantly disrupting global supply chains, equity markets, and the broader economic recovery from 2025-26 Iran war disruption. This scenario produces the strongest pressure for genuine allied coalition management, potentially forcing a more institutionally coherent American foreign policy by necessity rather than design.

Scenario Three: Ukraine Frozen Conflict Formalisation (20% probability)

A partial ceasefire arrangement in Ukraine is formalised enough to be described domestically as a "peace deal," with Trump claiming vindication of his promise to end the war even as the underlying territorial and sovereignty disputes remain entirely unresolved. European security guarantees under the coalition of the willing framework provide nominal cover for a settlement that neither Ukraine nor Russia formally endorses as permanent. This produces a "Korea model" - a frozen conflict with an ambiguous status that prevents full-scale war resumption while leaving the underlying causes of the conflict intact.

Scenario Four: Taiwan Crisis and Doctrine Test (10% probability)

A Chinese military action against Taiwan - whether a full blockade, seizure of outlying islands, or a more limited ADIZ enforcement operation - forces the Trump administration into its most consequential foreign policy decision: whether to treat its studied ambiguity on Taiwan as the beginning of a de facto accommodation with Chinese regional primacy, or to commit American military force in a crisis that would dwarf every other foreign policy action of the second term. This scenario, assessed as low probability but extremely high consequence, would determine whether the Trump doctrine's transactional framework can hold under conditions of genuine great power military confrontation - the question the entire administration has thus far managed to avoid answering directly.

Intelligence Forecast

Global Chanakya's twelve-to-eighteen month assessment centers on five converging dynamics that will shape Trump's foreign policy trajectory through the midterm cycle and beyond.

First, expect domestic political calculations to increasingly override strategic logic in foreign policy decisions as November 2026 midterms approach - the need to generate politically frameable wins, combined with the administration's demonstrated preference for dramatic unilateral action over sustained multilateral process, creates a structural bias toward escalation and disruption at precisely the moment when every major theatre demands sustained, patient diplomatic management. Watch particularly for Iran MOU management, where any breakdown of the sixty-day provisions creates immediate pressure for military re-engagement that would dominate the pre-midterm news environment.

Second, expect the US-China technology competition to intensify even within the trade truce's nominal framework - additional Entity List designations, restrictions on Chinese firms' access to American capital markets, and continued pressure on third-country suppliers to Chinese technology companies will continue as bipartisan instruments that the administration can deploy without touching the tariff truce's explicit terms. China's response - continued acceleration of domestic AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency under the 15th Five-Year Plan - will compound the competitive challenge regardless of any trade negotiation's outcome.

Third, watch the US dollar and American debt markets as the most sensitive leading indicators of whether the tariff-funded fiscal strategy is sustainable. Watch for signs of eroding US dollar dominance as the clearest early warning signal that the administration's foreign economic policy is generating costs that the domestic political narrative has not yet absorbed.

Fourth, expect India to be one of the more consequential beneficiaries of the Trump era's restructuring of global supply chains - the combination of tariff pressure on China, the administration's interest in alternative semiconductor manufacturing locations, and America's sustained Indo-Pacific focus on India as a Quad cornerstone creates genuine economic opportunity for New Delhi alongside the obvious political risks of Trump's volatility. India's challenge is to capture that opportunity without becoming structurally dependent on American good offices that the tariff crisis demonstrated can be withdrawn with minimal warning.

Fifth, and most broadly: Trump could take steps in 2026 that reinforce US alliances, or he could give autocratic adversaries even more reason to test US resolve. The outcome of that binary is not predetermined, and it will be determined less by any single policy decision than by whether the administration's midterm political pressures push it toward the kind of demonstrable strength that consolidates deterrence, or the kind of erratic unilateralism that invites adversarial testing of the gaps between American rhetoric and American commitment.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Donald Trump's foreign policy doctrine has done something genuinely rare in the history of American statecraft: it has disrupted the established international order's assumptions so thoroughly, across so many dimensions simultaneously, that even its most sophisticated critics cannot confidently predict what a return to "normal" would look like or whether the disrupted equilibria can be restored at all. The international trade order was thrown into disarray, and trade deals were explicitly linked to US national security interests. The administration did not abandon its key alliances, but it also made no clear indication that it would work toward a shared agenda. That ambiguity - allied but not committed, engaged but not reliable, powerful but unpredictable - is simultaneously the doctrine's greatest source of leverage and its most dangerous long-term vulnerability. For every capital navigating a Trump-shaped world, the practical strategic lesson is unambiguous: build the institutional and economic resilience to function without predictable American commitment, while maintaining close enough engagement with Washington to benefit from American power when it aligns with your own interests. Because in the Trump era, American foreign policy is not a system you can rely on - it is a weather pattern you must adapt to.

title: Benjamin Netanyahu's Regional Strategy 2026: The Super-Sparta Doctrine
excerpt: A definitive 2026 intelligence assessment of Benjamin Netanyahu's regional strategy - the Super-Sparta doctrine, the Iran war he engineered, the Gaza endgame he is delaying, Lebanon's open wound, a looming election, and a leader who has made permanent warfare the architecture of his own political survival.
content:
Benjamin Netanyahu's Regional Strategy 2026: The Super-Sparta Doctrine

To understand Benjamin Netanyahu's regional strategy in 2026, you have to begin with a recognition that most Western analysis refuses to make explicit: for this Prime Minister, the strategic and the personal are not separable. Every major military decision of the past two years - the resumption of full-scale Gaza combat in March 2025 after a ceasefire pause, the lobbying campaign that persuaded Donald Trump to authorise Operation Epic Fury against Iran's leadership, the deliberate non-closure of the Lebanon campaign despite multiple ceasefire opportunities, the refusal to define or deliver a credible endgame in Gaza - has served Netanyahu's geopolitical vision of a permanently reshaped Middle East simultaneously with his personal requirement to remain in office, avoid judicial accountability, and manage a coalition of far-right partners who would collapse his government the moment he appeared to be winding the wars down. The strategic and the political have become indistinguishable, and any analysis that tries to separate them produces a distorted picture of what is actually driving Israeli decision-making at the highest level.

This does not reduce Netanyahu to a cartoon villain, and this report does not treat him as one. He is, by most measures, the most consequential Israeli strategic thinker of his generation - a leader who has spent nearly two decades accumulating a sophisticated, original, and internally consistent worldview about Israel's security environment and what it requires. The problem Global Chanakya examines in this report is what happens when that worldview fuses with personal political survival in ways that make it genuinely impossible, from the outside, to determine where the strategic calculation ends and the self-preservation instinct begins.

Executive Summary

Benjamin Netanyahu enters the second half of 2026 as Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, having presided over the most consequential transformation of the Middle East's regional security architecture since the 1979 Iranian revolution - and having done so in a single eighteen-month window of extraordinary military activity that has killed Iran's Supreme Leader, devastated Hezbollah's operational capacity, eliminated successive Hamas military commanders, and reshaped the governance question in Gaza through the contested Board of Peace architecture. In early 2026, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lobbied President Donald Trump for a joint military strike on Iran, specifically targeting its leadership. Following high-level meetings in February, Trump authorized Operation Epic Fury, with reports citing Israeli intelligence provided by Netanyahu as a decisive factor in the decision.

At the same time, Netanyahu faces a convergence of pressures that would have terminated most political careers: an active International Criminal Court arrest warrant for war crimes and crimes against humanity that has curtailed his international travel and framed his diplomatic relationships; ongoing corruption cases for breach of trust, fraud, and bribery that have been his central legal preoccupation since 2020; a domestic polling environment showing his coalition collapsing toward minority territory ahead of an election that his own parliament has moved to advance; and a growing gap between public support for the wars' stated objectives and deepening public resentment at the government's inability to define or deliver a decisive end-state on any front.

The concept that crystallises his 2026 strategic posture better than any other is his own: the "Super-Sparta" model - a vision of Israel as a society in a state of permanent military readiness, normalising extended military service, sustained multi-front warfare of varying intensity, and high-alert civilian mobilisation as structural features of national life rather than temporary emergency measures. His concept of Super-Sparta - a society in a state of eternal military readiness - has moved from a rhetorical provocation to a concrete policy framework. The government is currently signalling an intent to normalise extended military service and a permanent high-alert status for the civilian economy. The analytical question this report addresses is whether Super-Sparta is a sustainable strategic model for a democracy of nine million people, or whether it is, at its core, a framework designed primarily to sustain a political leader whose personal survival depends on the continuation of conditions that make electoral accountability difficult and coalition alternatives implausible.

Background

Netanyahu's strategic worldview was formed through a lifetime of engagement with existential security questions that is, by any measure, more intellectually serious and more personally experienced than that of any other current Western or Middle Eastern leader. His brother Yonatan was killed leading the 1976 Entebbe rescue operation; he served in Sayeret Matkal, Israel's elite special forces unit; he spent years as a diplomat making Israel's security case in Washington; and he has governed Israel, across multiple non-consecutive terms totalling nearly nineteen years, through every major security crisis from Oslo's aftermath to the Second Intifada to multiple Gaza conflicts to the Abraham Accords to October 7.

The core of his worldview is a reading of Iranian hegemonic ambition as the organising threat to Israeli - and regional - security, combined with a deep scepticism of negotiated restraint as a durable solution to existential threats. Netanyahu's 2015 address to the US Congress opposing the JCPOA was widely mocked at the time as political theatre; his warning that a nuclear-hedging Iran with a preserved enrichment infrastructure would eventually produce a weapons-capable state has been substantially vindicated by subsequent events. His argument that the "Axis of Resistance" - Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis, and Iranian-backed Iraqi militias - constituted a structural threat requiring military rather than diplomatic management has similarly been proved at least partially correct by the decade of events that followed.

What has evolved, particularly since October 7, is the doctrine's relationship to democratic accountability. The security failures of October 7 - which Netanyahu has never fully accounted for publicly, despite the Shin Bet's own report placing significant blame on the government's policy choices - represented an existential threat to his political career that could only be managed through the kind of sustained, multi-front military activity that simultaneously addressed the underlying security threats and created the conditions under which holding him democratically accountable became politically complicated. Netanyahu's most immediate concern is delaying or ending the court cases against him for breach of trust, fraud, and bribery. The current Gaza war afforded the Prime Minister a unique strategic opening, which he has leveraged effectively. The war forced the court to postpone his hearings for more than fourteen months. Understanding this is not to reduce his strategic choices to cynicism - many of them represent genuine and defensible security judgments - but to understand the full architecture of incentives shaping his decision-making.

Current Situation

The Iran War: A Strategy Netanyahu Built

Of all the major military actions of 2026, Operation Epic Fury most directly reflects Netanyahu's strategic agency and personal diplomatic investment. According to multiple diplomatic sources, Netanyahu lobbied U.S. President Donald Trump to initiate the joint strikes. Reports cite Israeli intelligence provided by Netanyahu as a decisive factor in Trump's decision. The operation was, in essential ways, his operation - the culmination of years of intelligence preparation, diplomatic groundwork, and sustained lobbying of American administrations to treat Iran's nuclear and proxy infrastructure as an active rather than prospective threat requiring military rather than diplomatic resolution.

The strategic logic Netanyahu presented to Trump reflected his longstanding "mowing the grass" doctrine applied at its most ambitious scale: Israel is using this strategy against Hamas and Hezbollah with devastating effect. Not only is this war seriously degrading Iran's military and political power, it also represents a huge boon for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an election year. Hamas's 2023 attacks on Israel were an enormous embarrassment to the prime minister, who staked his reputation on being seen as the "protector of Israel". Killing Khamenei, eliminating Ali Larijani, and degrading Iran's nuclear command structure in a single operation addressed both the strategic problem Netanyahu had been warning about for two decades and the political problem of restoring his "Mr. Security" credentials after October 7's catastrophic failure.

The operation's strategic achievements are genuine. Iran's Axis of Resistance has been structurally degraded across all its major components simultaneously - Hezbollah devastated in Lebanon, Hamas's military leadership repeatedly decapitated in Gaza, Iran's own command and nuclear leadership eliminated. The installation of the IRGC-backed Mojtaba Khamenei as Supreme Leader, devoid of his father's religious authority and dependent on the Guards' institutional support, has produced exactly the kind of post-revolutionary legitimacy crisis that Netanyahu's allies argue will eventually generate Iranian domestic regime change. And the broader regional environment - the UAE exiting OPEC to align more closely with American energy policy, Israel and Lebanon entering what American officials described as "historic direct talks" during the Iran war's diplomatic phase, Gulf states quietly relieved of one of their central security anxieties - has moved in directions broadly consistent with Netanyahu's stated regional vision.

But the strategic costs are equally real, and Netanyahu's government has been considerably more candid about the achievements than the costs. Simply surviving the onslaught is considered a victory by these actors, given the vast differences in military capability. It has also led to the installation of a younger, emboldened, and more hardline leadership, especially in Iran, making the revitalisation of a more militant Axis of Resistance intent on exacting revenge more likely. Iran's decapitation has not produced the popular revolution against the clerical system that Netanyahu and Trump both publicly encouraged Iranians to mount; it has produced a security apparatus consolidation under IRGC control that, as Global Chanakya's Iran intelligence report assesses in detail, is likely to generate a more coercive and less diplomatically flexible Iranian state than the one it replaced.

Lebanon: The War That Will Not Close

Netanyahu's Lebanon strategy in 2026 captures the Super-Sparta model's logic and its limits simultaneously. In April 2026, Netanyahu said "There is no ceasefire in Lebanon." This statement - made months after the Islamabad MOU had nominally ended the wider Iran-Israel conflict - is the clearest possible articulation of a leader who views Lebanon's open wound as strategically preferable to any settlement that requires Hezbollah's disarmament to be verified before Israeli forces withdraw.

The IDF's continued ground campaign north of the Litani River, the siege of Bint Jbeil, the displacement of over a million Lebanese civilians, and the systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure in what Israeli officials describe as "terror infrastructure" elimination have achieved genuine military results - over a thousand confirmed Hezbollah operative losses, degradation of the rocket and missile stockpiles that posed the most immediate threat to northern Israel - while generating the most intense international humanitarian and legal scrutiny Israel has faced since 2006. Defence Minister Katz's explicit comparison of Lebanon to Gaza - vowing to "eliminate the threat just as we did in Gaza, including demolishing homes" - captures a doctrine of comprehensive destruction that, whatever its military rationale, carries enormous diplomatic and legal costs that Netanyahu's government has largely chosen to absorb rather than constrain.

The strategic rationale for keeping Lebanon open is straightforward in Netanyahu's framework: an unconditional withdrawal, without verified Hezbollah disarmament, would reconstitute the threat within years and require another, costlier conflict. The tactical military logic holds. What it does not address is the governance question: Israel is sustaining a ground campaign that has displaced twenty percent of Lebanon's population inside a country with no functioning central government capable of providing the kind of authoritative security commitment that would make an Israeli withdrawal strategically rational. This is the structural trap of the Lebanon campaign - Netanyahu's own stated exit condition (Hezbollah disarmament) requires a political interlocutor that does not exist inside Lebanon's fractured governance environment, leaving the IDF in an indefinite occupation that strains reserves, accumulates international condemnation, and has, as Chatham House's April 2026 analysis notes, produced Israeli public awareness that "strategic fatigue" is setting in without a decisive end-state anywhere in sight.

Gaza: The Endgame Netanyahu Refuses to Define

Gaza is where the fusion of strategic vision and political self-preservation is most clearly visible, and most analytically important to understand precisely. The October 2025 ceasefire, phase two's framework, and the Board of Peace architecture that Netanyahu joined in January 2026 despite his active ICC arrest warrant all reflect a leader playing a double game: appearing engaged in a diplomatic resolution process while simultaneously ensuring that the conditions for any resolution - Hamas disarmament, withdrawal to the "yellow line," an international stabilisation force - remain structurally out of reach.

Palestinians see Netanyahu as an obstacle to any attempt for the Trump administration to move forward to phase two. They believe Netanyahu's only interest in the second phase is to implement the disarmament of Hamas, while he remains uninterested in withdrawing troops beyond the so-called yellow line - another key element. This assessment, while politically framed, is strategically accurate. Netanyahu's Gaza approach has consistently applied maximum military pressure - the targeted killings of Hamas military chief Izz al-Din Haddad and his successor Mohammed Odeh, the continued expansion of Israeli controlled territory from 53% to approximately 60% of the Strip - while refusing to articulate a governance endpoint that does not amount to indefinite Israeli military control. Secretary of State Rubio's own public acknowledgement that Netanyahu's 70% territory control target "contradicts" Trump's peace plan is perhaps the most candid American statement yet of the daylight between Washington and Jerusalem on Gaza's actual future.

The domestic political logic is unmistakable. Netanyahu's coalition is composed of far-right partners for whom any withdrawal from Gaza that does not produce Hamas's total elimination and does not preserve Israeli settlement rights in the Strip represents a coalition-ending betrayal. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has explicitly opposed the Board of Peace as an institution and advocated for unilateral Israeli sovereignty over Gaza's future. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir - against whom the ICC prosecutor's office has reportedly secretly requested arrest warrants alongside Smotrich - represents a faction that views any concession on Gaza governance as existentially threatening to the settlement project and to their own political futures. Managing these partners while maintaining enough engagement with Washington's peace framework to avoid complete American disengagement is Netanyahu's central coalition management challenge of 2026.

The ICC Warrant: A Career-Defining Legal Cloud

The ICC's November 2024 arrest warrant against Netanyahu - the first against the leader of a Western-backed democratic country - has become a structural feature of his strategic environment rather than a passing controversy. Netanyahu skipped the 56th World Economic Forum at Davos 2026 to avoid the arrest warrant, as Switzerland is a Rome Statute signatory. This single decision captures the warrant's practical impact on his freedom of movement: one of the world's most important annual gatherings of global economic and political leadership has become inaccessible to the sitting Israeli Prime Minister.

The warrant's cascade of consequences extends considerably further. All 125 ICC member states are required to arrest Netanyahu and Gallant if they enter their territory. In practice, this means Netanyahu's diplomatic travel is functionally restricted to non-ICC member states - the United States, Hungary (whose then-outgoing Prime Minister Orbán explicitly refused to enforce the warrant during Netanyahu's 2025 visit), and a limited set of other states outside the Rome Statute's jurisdiction. In May 2026, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and ordered the South Korean government to make a judgement on whether to issue an arrest warrant in accordance with the ICC warrant - a sign that the warrant's active enforcement is expanding rather than contracting as the political shock of its issuance fades.

The legal file extends beyond the ICC. Netanyahu's domestic corruption trial - paused repeatedly during wartime security emergencies - continues to await his testimony, with lawyers estimating the process could extend through 2026. In February 2026, the Attorney General and Cabinet Legal Advisor summoned Netanyahu to provide explanations regarding an investigation into the leak of classified documents to the German newspaper Bild. The case reportedly concerns attempts to obstruct investigations into the leak of sensitive Israeli documents. Netanyahu's chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, was arrested on suspicion of attempting to impede the investigative process. The domestic legal pressure, far from diminishing as war fatigue sets in, is intensifying - adding a new obstruction dimension to the existing fraud and corruption proceedings that have defined Netanyahu's legal reality since 2020.

The Election: Super-Sparta Meets Democratic Reality

Netanyahu's most immediate political challenge is an election that his own coalition has moved to advance, now expected as early as September 2026. An April 16 Haaretz/Channel 12 poll projects the current coalition would plummet to 51 seats in the Knesset in an election held now. The opposition has surged to a formidable 69 seats - including Arab parties - while the Jewish opposition holds 59 seats, putting it on the cusp of a majority without requiring a coalition with non-Zionist factions. These numbers represent the sharpest electoral deterioration of Netanyahu's coalition since the war began, driven by precisely the dynamic that Chatham House analysts have identified: public support for the war's objectives sits alongside increasing resentment at the government's inability to define or deliver a decisive end-state. The governing coalition is unable to use the war to grow its support.

Netanyahu's electoral strategy, consistent with his entire post-October 7 political management, is to prevent a settlement on any front that would remove the emergency conditions sustaining his political position, while simultaneously appearing engaged in enough diplomatic process to avoid the complete collapse of international support that would make Israel's security position untenable. The Super-Sparta model's political function is to make permanent warfare appear not as a failure of strategic resolution but as a deliberate, sophisticated doctrine of national security - a reframing of indefinite multi-front conflict as strategic choice rather than political inability to conclude.

Strategic Analysis

Netanyahu's regional strategy rests on three intellectual pillars that deserve separate assessment. The first is the "mowing the grass" doctrine - the concept that Israel cannot eliminate the threats it faces but can periodically degrade them through military action, accepting the recurring cost of each operation as preferable to the alternative of allowing adversaries to accumulate capability between conflicts. Applied at the scale of 2025-26 - multiple simultaneous campaigns against Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas, and the broader Axis of Resistance - it has produced genuinely impressive results in terms of capability degradation. Its central strategic weakness, as any honest assessment must acknowledge, is that it explicitly accepts the indefinite recurrence of conflict rather than resolving the political conditions that generate it. Super-Sparta is, in essence, mowing the grass elevated to a national vision - and no society has permanently sustained that posture without either resolving the underlying conflict or eventually exhausting itself.

The second pillar is the Abraham Accords framework as the alternative to Palestinian state resolution - the concept that Israel can achieve strategic normalisation with the Arab world through economic and security arrangements with Arab governments that do not require resolving the Palestinian question at the level of sovereignty. The accords represented a genuine strategic innovation when originally achieved in 2020. But the continued slaughter of Palestinians in Gaza, the attempts to destabilise Egypt and Jordan through continued insistence on ethnic cleansing, and the military incursions into and occupations of Syria and Lebanon do not contribute to the Abraham Accords' aims of regional stability and prosperity. Saudi Arabia's own stated conditions for normalisation - a "credible pathway" to Palestinian statehood - remain publicly unchanged despite the wars' reshaping of the regional landscape, and Netanyahu's Gaza strategy has made meeting those conditions domestically impossible as long as his current coalition remains in place.

The third pillar is the strategic relationship with Washington as the indispensable guarantor of Israel's freedom of military action. Netanyahu's management of Trump is the most sophisticated bilateral relationship he has maintained through 2026 - feeding Trump's intelligence, framing joint operations as Trump's achievements, accepting the Board of Peace role despite the ICC warrant to maintain Washington's patronage, and calibrating every public statement about Gaza to avoid the specific formulations that might trigger Trump's mercurial impatience with the conflict's resolution. Whether this relationship can survive a midterm environment in which Trump's domestic political needs increasingly diverge from Netanyahu's military timeline - particularly on Gaza, where Rubio's own public acknowledgement of contradiction between Netanyahu's territory targets and Trump's peace plan signals genuine strain - is the central diplomatic question of Netanyahu's 2026 remainder.

Global Impact

Netanyahu's regional strategy in 2026 has reshaped the Middle East's strategic architecture in ways that extend well beyond Israel's immediate security environment. The killing of Khamenei and the degradation of the Axis of Resistance have reduced Iran's capacity for regional coercion, benefiting Gulf states whose own security calculus has long been dominated by Iranian proxy threat. The UAE's exit from OPEC and its alignment with American energy policy during the Iran war is partly a consequence of that reduced threat calculus - a Gulf state willing to take positions it could not previously afford when Iranian retaliation capacity was higher. For India, the reshaping of the Gulf security environment carries direct consequences: both the energy security exposure that any sustained Hormuz disruption creates and the diplomatic complexity of maintaining the India-Israel relationship alongside India's carefully cultivated Gulf partnerships simultaneously.

The ICC warrant's expanding enforcement - with South Korea's May 2026 presidential statement calling Netanyahu a "war criminal" marking the first significant Indo-Pacific state to actively apply the framework - represents a different dimension of global impact: the progressive erosion of the legal insulation that American political support has historically provided for Israeli military conduct. As more states in Asia, Africa, and Latin America take positions consistent with the ICC framework, the diplomatic space available for Israeli military operations narrowed even as the operations' immediate military effectiveness remained high. This is a long-term structural constraint on Israeli strategic freedom of action that no military success of the current campaign cycle has resolved.

For the broader rules-based international order, Netanyahu's 2026 conduct presents a fundamental challenge: the first leader of a Western-backed democracy to operate under an active ICC arrest warrant has continued to govern, to wage major military campaigns, to join international governance bodies, and to sustain an active alliance with the world's most powerful state without facing any material consequence from the warrant's existence beyond travel restriction. The precedent this sets - for how other democratic leaders might calculate the relationship between military conduct and international legal accountability - is one of the most consequential institutional developments of the current era, with implications that extend far beyond the Middle East.

Risk Assessment

  • Electoral defeat ending the Super-Sparta model: April polling shows the coalition plummeting to 49-51 seats while the opposition commands 59-69 seats. An opposition victory - particularly one requiring coalition with centre-left parties opposed to the current war's conduct - would produce the most abrupt reversal of Israeli regional strategy in decades, with direct consequences for Gaza governance, Lebanon withdrawal timelines, and the pace of any Iran-related diplomatic engagement.
  • Trump support erosion over Gaza: The public gap between Netanyahu's 70% Gaza territory control target and Trump's own peace plan, acknowledged by Secretary of State Rubio, represents a live fault line in the relationship that Israeli continued settlement expansion in the West Bank and Hamas's refusal to disarm are likely to widen. Trump's domestic midterm pressures could produce the kind of publicly expressed presidential frustration - as has happened episodically before - that constrains Netanyahu's military options at a critical political moment.
  • ICC warrant enforcement escalation: As additional ICC member states activate or signal activation of enforcement obligations - the South Korea precedent in May 2026 is significant precisely because it comes from the Indo-Pacific rather than Europe or Latin America - Netanyahu's diplomatic travel restrictions could extend to affect the bilateral relationships that Israel's security architecture depends on maintaining.
  • Coalition collapse over Board of Peace: Smotrich and Ben-Gvir's explicit opposition to the Board of Peace framework and their maximalist Gaza positions create constant coalition fragility, particularly if a Trump-brokered phase two settlement moves toward any form of international governance of Gaza that does not include Israeli military control as a permanent feature.
  • Iranian reconstitution and revenge: The installation of a younger, emboldened, and more hardline leadership in Iran makes the revitalisation of a more militant Axis of Resistance intent on exacting revenge more likely. A successor Iranian leadership with nothing to lose diplomatically and institutional memory of the 2026 war's humiliation carries elevated risk of covert nuclear reconstitution and proxy network rebuilding - the exact strategic risk Netanyahu's Iran campaign was designed to prevent.
  • Reservist and societal exhaustion: The lack of a parliamentary majority and a sustainable solution to the manpower crisis means the government is overextending the very society it governs. A democratic society cannot sustain permanent multi-front warfare at current intensity indefinitely, and the reservoir of civic consent that has sustained Israeli public support for the wars' objectives is narrowing, not expanding, as end-states remain undefined on every front.
The Super-Sparta model's central contradiction is that it requires a society to permanently accept the costs of existential military mobilisation without the political resolution of the conflicts generating those costs - a demand that even Israel's remarkable societal resilience cannot satisfy indefinitely, and that Netanyahu's coalition's internal contradictions make it structurally incapable of delivering.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis

The following are illustrative projections based on current trajectories, structured for strategic stress-testing rather than presented as confirmed predictions.

Scenario One: Netanyahu Wins Election, Super-Sparta Continues (35% probability)

Netanyahu's Likud leads the polls, and while the current coalition polling is weak, the fragmented Israeli electoral system and the right-wing bloc's structural advantages allow him to assemble a new coalition - possibly with different far-right partners - that preserves his leadership. Gaza remains under partial Israeli military control without a resolved governance endpoint; Lebanon stabilises into a lower-intensity buffer zone arrangement with periodic Israeli strikes; Iran's nuclear file remains unverified and periodically volatile; and the Super-Sparta framework becomes, by necessity rather than design, the de facto permanent condition of Israeli strategic life through the remainder of the decade.

Scenario Two: Electoral Defeat and Strategic Recalibration (30% probability)

Opposition polling leads translate into an electoral result that produces a government without Netanyahu, led by a centre-left or centrist coalition that includes parties explicitly committed to defined Gaza withdrawal timelines, accelerated Lebanon disengagement, and a more active engagement with the Palestinian governance question as a precondition for Saudi normalisation. This scenario produces significant short-term regional uncertainty - particularly regarding whether Hezbollah uses an Israeli withdrawal to reconstitute capability - but potentially opens diplomatic pathways that Netanyahu's coalition has structurally foreclosed.

Scenario Three: Coalition Collapse Before Election (20% probability)

Smotrich or Ben-Gvir withdraw from the coalition over Gaza Board of Peace phase two terms or Lebanon ceasefire terms before the election date, triggering an earlier and more chaotic electoral process than current planning assumes, with greater uncertainty about coalition arithmetic and potentially producing a transitional government of limited mandate that cannot make the major strategic decisions Gaza and Lebanon require.

Scenario Four: ICC Enforcement Crisis (15% probability)

A significant ICC member state - potentially a European ally facing domestic political pressure from courts enforcing the warrant - moves toward active enforcement in a way that creates a genuine diplomatic crisis between Israel and a key European partner, testing whether the Trump administration's political support for Netanyahu can prevent the warrant's practical effect on Israel's European relationships from becoming materially damaging to Israeli strategic interests.

Intelligence Forecast

Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on five converging dynamics that will define whether Netanyahu's Super-Sparta model consolidates as Israel's permanent strategic framework or fractures under the accumulated weight of its own contradictions.

First, watch the Israeli election with exceptional analytical attention - the outcome will determine not just who governs Israel, but whether the Super-Sparta model's assumption of indefinite multi-front conflict management as national policy survives democratic accountability or is replaced by a government with both the mandate and the incentive to pursue defined closure on at least one major front. Second, expect the Board of Peace to remain functionally performative rather than operationally decisive through 2026, with Netanyahu using it as international legitimacy cover without accepting the phase two governance architecture that would require genuine withdrawal or Hamas disarmament verification. Third, expect the ICC warrant's diplomatic consequences to compound slowly but consistently - each new state that activates enforcement language narrows Netanyahu's international operating space in ways that are strategically significant even if no physical arrest occurs. Fourth, watch the Trump relationship for signs of genuine rather than rhetorical strain - the Rubio acknowledgement of contradiction on Gaza territory targets is the clearest signal yet that the unconditional American support Netanyahu has relied on is becoming conditional in ways his coalition arithmetic makes it very difficult to accommodate. Fifth, expect Iran's post-war reconstitution trajectory to be the long-horizon strategic variable that ultimately determines whether Netanyahu's Iran campaign achieved durable strategic objectives or merely expensive temporary degradation - the absence of verified inspection mechanisms in the Islamabad MOU creates a recurring intelligence and policy crisis trigger that will demand ongoing Israeli decision-making regardless of who governs after the October elections.

For India and the wider Indo-Pacific, Netanyahu's regional strategy carries practical implications that deserve direct attention. India's growing defence and technology relationship with Israel has provided genuine strategic value - Israeli drone technology, cyber capability, and intelligence cooperation have materially enhanced Indian military capacity - but has also accumulated diplomatic costs as India's Gulf partnerships require careful management against the backdrop of Israel's conduct in Gaza and Lebanon. As more Indo-Pacific states activate ICC enforcement language and as the international legal environment around Israeli military conduct becomes more actively contested, India's capacity to maintain its Israel relationship without accumulating disproportionate diplomatic costs with Arab and Muslim-majority partners will require more active and explicit management than the current posture of strategic ambiguity provides.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Benjamin Netanyahu's regional strategy in 2026 represents the most ambitious attempt by any Israeli leader to fundamentally reshape the Middle East's strategic architecture since the state's founding - and the most sustained fusion of genuine strategic vision with personal political survival calculation in contemporary international politics. He has achieved things that were, two years ago, genuinely unthinkable: the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader, the effective dismantling of the Axis of Resistance's operational coherence, and the repositioning of Israel from a state managing an intractable conflict to one that has demonstrably changed the regional balance of power through military action. These achievements are real, and the strategic logic behind them - however brutally executed and however costly in human and diplomatic terms - is more sophisticated than its critics typically acknowledge. What Netanyahu has not achieved, and what the Super-Sparta doctrine structurally prevents him from achieving, is the conversion of military dominance into durable political resolution. On Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, the pattern is identical: overwhelming tactical success producing strategic ambiguity, because defining a clear political endpoint would require accommodating domestic coalition partners who benefit from the absence of one, just as Netanyahu himself benefits from the conditions that prevent the democratic accountability that four years of catastrophic decisions - beginning with the intelligence failure that allowed October 7 - still await.
